dead_battery.name: Weak or dead battery
dead_battery.plain: Your battery doesn't have enough power left to start the engine. Think of it like a phone at 1%.
dead_battery.drive: Yes, once it starts. If it needed a jump, drive 30+ minutes so it can recharge.
dead_battery.todo: Get a jump start, then have the battery tested. Most parts stores test it free in about 5 minutes.
dead_battery.summary: The battery doesn't have enough charge to spin the starter. Fast clicking, dim lights, or a slow crank are the classic signs, especially on cold mornings.
checks: Measure battery voltage with the truck off for an hour: 12.6V is full, 12.2V is about half, under 12.0V is flat.
Clean and tighten both terminals; white or green crust adds resistance. GM side-post bolts loosen and corrode often.
Have it load tested free at a parts store; most batteries last 3 to 5 years.
If it keeps dying, check for parasitic draw: under 50 mA with everything off (wait 30+ minutes for modules to sleep).
signs: Lights and radio are dimmer than usual
It started slower on cold mornings for a while
The battery is 3 to 5 years old or more
Power windows move slowly with the engine off

bad_starter.name: Bad starter or solenoid
bad_starter.plain: The starter is the small motor that spins the engine to get it going. The battery is fine, but the starter isn't doing its job.
bad_starter.drive: If it starts, yes, but it may leave you stranded next time. Don't shut it off somewhere you can't get help.
bad_starter.todo: Ask a shop or parts store to test the starter. Tell them: "one click, lights stay bright, engine doesn't turn."
bad_starter.summary: The battery is fine but the starter won't spin the engine. Usually one loud click, a grinding whir, or nothing at all when you turn the key.
checks: Confirm the battery reads 12.4V+ and the headlights stay bright while you try to start.
Single loud click with bright lights points to the starter solenoid or worn starter motor.
Check the small trigger wire at the starter gets 12V while someone holds the key in START.
GM trucks: the starter sits near the exhaust; heat soak can cause no-crank when hot. Check the main cable and ground strap to the block.
signs: Sometimes it starts and sometimes it just clicks
Tapping under the vehicle near the starter gets it to start
A grinding sound when you turn the key
Smell of burning or smoke from under the vehicle after trying to start

bad_alternator.name: Bad alternator / charging problem
bad_alternator.plain: The alternator recharges the battery while you drive. When it fails, the vehicle runs on the battery until it goes dead.
bad_alternator.drive: Only a short distance. It can die while driving, so head straight to a shop or home.
bad_alternator.todo: Have the charging system tested (free at most parts stores). Replacing a battery alone won't fix this.
bad_alternator.summary: The alternator isn't recharging the battery, so the truck runs off the battery until it dies. Battery light, dimming lights, and a whine that rises with RPM are common.
checks: With the engine running, battery voltage should be 13.8 to 14.7V. Under 13.2V means it isn't charging.
Turn on headlights, blower and rear defrost: voltage should stay above 13.2V at idle.
Check the serpentine belt is tight and not slipping on the alternator pulley.
Inspect the big output wire and fusible link at the alternator for corrosion or a loose nut.
signs: A new battery keeps dying
Headlights get brighter when you rev the engine
A whining sound that rises with the engine
A burning rubber or hot wire smell

worn_brake_pads.name: Worn brake pads
worn_brake_pads.plain: Brake pads are what squeeze to stop the wheels. They wear down over time, like an eraser.
worn_brake_pads.drive: Squealing: yes, but get it done soon. Grinding: only to a shop; it's metal on metal and gets worse fast.
worn_brake_pads.todo: Get a brake inspection. Fixing it early (pads only) costs much less than waiting until the rotors are ruined too.
worn_brake_pads.summary: The pad friction material is worn thin. A high squeal means the wear indicator is touching; grinding means metal on metal and the rotors are getting damaged.
checks: Look through the wheel at the pad: replace at 3 mm (about 1/8 in.) of material or less.
Grinding means the backing plate is on the rotor; replace pads and check rotors right away.
Check rotor thickness against the minimum stamped on the rotor.
Heavy 2500HD trucks and big tires wear pads faster; use a severe-duty or ceramic HD pad.
signs: A high squeal that stops when you press the brake harder
Takes a little longer to stop
Lots of dark dust on the front wheels
The brake pedal goes a bit lower than before

warped_rotors.name: Warped or uneven brake rotors
warped_rotors.plain: The rotors are the metal discs the brake pads squeeze. When they wear unevenly, you feel a pulse or shake while braking.
warped_rotors.drive: Yes, carefully. Brakes still work, just not as smoothly. Leave extra stopping room.
warped_rotors.todo: Ask a shop to check the rotors. They're often replaced together with the brake pads.
warped_rotors.summary: The rotors have uneven thickness, so the pads grab and release as the wheel turns. You feel it as a pulsing brake pedal or steering wheel shake only while braking.
checks: Feel for a pulsing pedal or wheel shake that happens only when braking, worst from highway speed.
Measure rotor runout with a dial indicator: over about 0.002 in. (0.05 mm) causes pulsing.
Check for blue heat spots or hard glazed patches on the rotor face.
Torque lug nuts in a star pattern to spec (GM 2500HD: 140 ft-lb); uneven impact-gun torque warps rotors.
signs: Shaking only when you brake
The brake pedal pulses under your foot
Worse when stopping from highway speed or going downhill
Started after new pads or hard braking

brake_fluid_leak.name: Brake fluid leak / hydraulic failure
brake_fluid_leak.plain: The brakes work by pushing fluid through lines. If fluid leaks out, the brakes can stop working.
brake_fluid_leak.drive: No. Don't drive it. Have it towed or fixed where it is.
brake_fluid_leak.todo: Call a tow or a mobile mechanic. Tell them the pedal feels soft or goes to the floor.
brake_fluid_leak.summary: Brake fluid is leaking or the hydraulic system is failing, so the brakes may stop working. A soft or sinking pedal is an emergency.
checks: Check the master cylinder level; it should be between MIN and MAX. Fluid is clear to amber and slippery.
Look for wet spots inside each wheel, at the calipers, and along the steel lines. GM steel brake lines rust through, especially above the fuel tank and frame rail.
Pedal that slowly sinks to the floor while held at a stop points to a leak or a bad master cylinder.
Do not drive. Have it towed or repaired in place.
signs: Brake pedal feels soft or spongy
Brake warning light on the dash
Wet spot near a wheel
You have to pump the brakes

bad_wheel_bearing.name: Bad wheel bearing / hub
bad_wheel_bearing.plain: Wheel bearings let each wheel spin smoothly. A worn one hums or growls, louder as you go faster.
bad_wheel_bearing.drive: Short trips at normal speed, yes, but get it fixed soon. A bad bearing can eventually let the wheel wobble or lock up.
bad_wheel_bearing.todo: Ask a shop to check the wheel bearings. Tell them which side the noise seems to come from and if it changes when you turn.
bad_wheel_bearing.summary: A worn wheel bearing makes a hum or growl that gets louder with speed and often changes when you swerve left or right.
checks: On a gentle curve, the noise usually gets louder when weight shifts onto the bad side.
Jack the wheel up, grab at 12 and 6 o'clock and rock it: any play or clunk means a worn bearing.
Spin the wheel by hand and feel the coil spring or strut for roughness.
GM 4WD hubs are a bolt-in unit; an ABS light can come on when the hub's sensor fails too. Lifts and big tires wear them faster.
signs: A hum like an airplane that gets louder with speed
Noise changes when you curve one way
ABS light can come on
Steering feels a little loose

worn_serpentine_belt.name: Worn serpentine belt or tensioner
worn_serpentine_belt.plain: A rubber belt on the front of the engine runs the charging, steering and cooling parts. When it's worn or loose, it squeals.
worn_serpentine_belt.drive: Yes for now. If it breaks, you'll lose power steering and charging and the engine can overheat, so don't wait long.
worn_serpentine_belt.todo: A belt is cheap and quick to replace. Ask for a belt and tensioner check.
worn_serpentine_belt.summary: The belt that drives the alternator, power steering and water pump is slipping or worn. It squeals at startup, in the cold, or when the A/C or steering loads it.
checks: Look for cracks across the ribs, glazing, chunks missing, or fraying edges.
Watch the tensioner arm with the engine running; it shouldn't bounce or flutter.
Spin each pulley by hand with the belt off: any wobble or rough noise is a bad idler or tensioner.
6.0L Vortec: check the routing sticker under the hood before removing it. Belt life is about 60,000 to 100,000 miles.
signs: Squeal at startup or in rain
Squeal when the A/C turns on
Cracks you can see on the belt
Battery or steering problems if it slips

engine_misfire.name: Engine misfire (plugs, wires, coils)
engine_misfire.plain: One of the engine's cylinders isn't firing right, usually from worn spark plugs or a bad ignition coil. The engine shakes and loses power.
engine_misfire.drive: Short distances if it's mild. If the check engine light is flashing, park it. Driving can damage expensive exhaust parts.
engine_misfire.todo: Get the code read (free at most parts stores). Spark plugs and coils are common, fairly cheap fixes.
engine_misfire.summary: One or more cylinders isn't firing properly, so the engine shakes, runs rough, and loses power. A flashing check engine light means a severe misfire that can damage the converter.
checks: Read the code: P0300 is random, P0301 to P0308 names the cylinder.
Swap the coil from the misfiring cylinder to another one; if the misfire follows the coil, replace the coil.
Pull plugs and check gap and condition. 6.0L Vortec spec is 0.040 in. Replace plug wires if they're burnt on the exhaust manifold.
If plugs and coils are fine, do a compression test (healthy cylinders within about 10% of each other).
signs: Shaking at stop lights
Check engine light, sometimes flashing
Loss of power going uphill
Worse gas mileage

dirty_maf_sensor.name: Dirty or failing MAF sensor
dirty_maf_sensor.plain: A sensor measures the air going into the engine. When it's dirty, the engine gets the wrong fuel mix and stumbles or hesitates.
dirty_maf_sensor.drive: Yes. It's annoying, not dangerous. Be careful pulling into traffic if it hesitates.
dirty_maf_sensor.todo: Cleaning the sensor with a $10 spray can fix it. Get the code read first to confirm.
dirty_maf_sensor.summary: The mass air flow sensor measures air going into the engine. When it's dirty the computer adds the wrong amount of fuel, causing hesitation, surging, stalling, or bad mileage.
checks: Read codes: P0101 to P0103 point straight at the MAF; P0171/P0174 lean codes can too.
Clean the sensor wire with MAF cleaner only (no touching, no other sprays) and let it dry fully.
Check the air filter and that the intake tube clamps are tight with no cracks after the sensor.
With a scan tool, MAF reading at warm idle on a 6.0L is roughly 5 to 8 g/s and should climb smoothly with RPM.
signs: Hesitates or stumbles when you press the gas
Stalls right after starting
Worse gas mileage
Idle goes up and down

vacuum_leak.name: Vacuum leak
vacuum_leak.plain: Air is sneaking into the engine through a cracked hose or gasket. The engine idles high or rough and may hiss.
vacuum_leak.drive: Yes. Get it checked so it doesn't cause bigger problems over time.
vacuum_leak.todo: Ask a shop for a "smoke test". It finds the leak fast. Often it's just a cheap cracked hose.
vacuum_leak.summary: Air is sneaking into the engine past the MAF sensor, so it runs lean. Expect a high or rough idle, a hissing sound, and lean codes P0171/P0174.
checks: Listen for a hiss around the intake manifold, PCV hoses and brake booster hose with the engine idling.
Spray carb cleaner or use a smoke test around gaskets; an idle change shows the leak.
Check long term fuel trims: over +10% at idle that drops at higher RPM points to a vacuum leak.
6.0L Vortec: check the PCV hoses, intake manifold gaskets, and the brake booster check valve grommet.
signs: Idles high or rough
A hissing sound at idle
Check engine light for 'lean'
Brake pedal feels harder than usual

fuel_delivery_problem.name: Fuel delivery problem (pump, filter, pressure)
fuel_delivery_problem.plain: The engine isn't getting enough fuel, often from a weak fuel pump or clogged fuel filter.
fuel_delivery_problem.drive: Risky. It can stall while driving, including on the highway. Avoid long trips until it's checked.
fuel_delivery_problem.todo: Ask a shop to test fuel pressure. Mention if it cranks normally but won't start, or loses power going uphill.
fuel_delivery_problem.summary: The engine isn't getting enough fuel pressure. It may crank but not start, lose power going uphill or under load, or sputter at highway speed.
checks: Turn the key to ON and listen for the pump to hum for about 2 seconds from the tank.
Test fuel pressure at the rail Schrader valve: GM Vortec trucks want about 55 to 62 psi, holding steady under load.
Replace the inline fuel filter on the frame rail if it's old; it's a cheap first step on these trucks.
Check the fuel pump relay and fuse. A tap on the tank while cranking that makes it start points to a dying pump.
signs: Takes a long time to start
Loses power going uphill or towing
Sputters at highway speed
Starts fine with a full tank but not a low one

overheating.name: Engine overheating
overheating.plain: The engine is too hot. Coolant is low, leaking, or not flowing. Heat can wreck an engine in minutes.
overheating.drive: No. Pull over safely and turn it off. Don't open the radiator cap while hot.
overheating.todo: Let it cool at least 30 minutes. Check the coolant level, then get it towed or checked before driving far.
overheating.summary: The engine is running too hot. Driving an overheating engine can warp the heads or blow the head gasket in minutes.
checks: Pull over and shut it off. Never open the radiator cap hot; wait until the hose is soft and cool.
Check coolant level in the reservoir and radiator, and look for leaks at hoses, water pump weep hole and radiator.
Make sure the cooling fan clutch engages: a hot engine should make the fan roar and be hard to spin (engine OFF).
Look for bubbles in the coolant or milky oil, which points to a head gasket. Normal 6.0L temp is about 195 to 220°F.
signs: Temperature needle climbing toward hot
Steam from under the hood
Sweet smell
Heater blowing cold while the engine is hot

thermostat_stuck_open.name: Thermostat stuck open
thermostat_stuck_open.plain: A part called the thermostat controls engine temperature. Stuck open, the engine never fully warms up, so heat is weak.
thermostat_stuck_open.drive: Yes. It's not urgent, but you'll get weak heat and worse gas mileage.
thermostat_stuck_open.todo: A thermostat is a fairly cheap part. Ask a shop to replace it.
thermostat_stuck_open.summary: The thermostat isn't closing, so the engine never warms up fully. Weak heat, a temp gauge that stays low, worse mileage, and code P0128 are typical.
checks: Watch the temp gauge: it should reach about 195 to 210°F within 10 to 15 minutes of driving.
Look for code P0128 (coolant temp below thermostat temp).
Feel the upper radiator hose early in warm-up: if it warms right away with the engine cold, the thermostat is open.
A thermostat is a cheap part; replace the gasket with it and bleed air from the system after.
signs: Heater only blows lukewarm
Temperature needle stays low
Worse gas mileage in winter
Takes forever to warm up

transmission_problem.name: Transmission problem
transmission_problem.plain: The transmission changes gears. Slipping, late, or hard shifts mean it's struggling, often from low or old fluid.
transmission_problem.drive: Gently and only if needed. Avoid towing or hard acceleration. Driving it slipping makes it worse fast.
transmission_problem.todo: Have the fluid checked first; it's often the cheapest fix. Then get the codes read at a transmission shop.
transmission_problem.summary: The transmission is slipping, shifting late or hard, or not engaging gears. Catching it early with a fluid and code check can save a rebuild.
checks: Check fluid level hot with the engine running in park. It should be red and not smell burnt.
Read codes: P0700 range and P0894 (slipping) are common. Low fluid often causes the slipping.
4L80E/4L60E: a slip between 1st and 2nd or flare on the 2-3 shift is common; a fluid and filter service is the first step.
Bigger tires on a lifted truck add load; check the speedometer is recalibrated so the shift points are right.
signs: Engine revs but you don't speed up
Hard or late shifts
A delay when you shift into drive
Red fluid under the middle of the vehicle

worn_cv_axle.name: Worn CV axle
worn_cv_axle.plain: A CV axle connects a front wheel to the engine. When its joint wears out, it clicks when you turn.
worn_cv_axle.drive: Yes for now. If it breaks, the wheel stops getting power, so don't wait months.
worn_cv_axle.todo: Ask a shop to replace the CV axle. It's a common, moderate repair.
worn_cv_axle.summary: The constant velocity joint on a front axle is worn. It clicks or pops when turning sharply, usually after the rubber boot tears and the grease leaks out.
checks: Turn the wheel fully one way and drive slowly in a circle: clicking that gets faster with speed is a worn outer CV joint.
Look at the rubber boots for tears and grease slung on the inside of the wheel and frame.
Lifted 4WD trucks run the CV axles at a steeper angle, which wears boots and joints faster.
A clunk on acceleration can be a worn inner joint; check for in-and-out play.
signs: Clicking when turning in a parking lot
Grease slung inside the front wheel
Clunk when you speed up
Vibration when accelerating

worn_u_joint.name: Worn U-joint (driveshaft)
worn_u_joint.plain: U-joints are the flexible joints in the driveshaft under the truck. Worn ones clunk and squeak.
worn_u_joint.drive: Short trips. A broken U-joint can drop the driveshaft while moving, so get it fixed soon.
worn_u_joint.todo: U-joints are cheap parts. Ask a shop to check the driveshaft joints, especially on a lifted truck.
worn_u_joint.summary: A universal joint in the driveshaft is worn. It clunks when shifting into gear, squeaks at low speed, and causes a vibration that gets worse with speed.
checks: Under the truck (parked, wheels chocked) grab the driveshaft near each U-joint and twist and lift: any play means it's worn.
Look for rust dust around the bearing caps, a sign the needle bearings are dry.
Lifted trucks change the driveshaft angles, so U-joints wear much faster. Grease the zerk fittings if yours have them.
Don't wait: a failed U-joint can drop the driveshaft at speed.
signs: Clunk when shifting into drive or reverse
Squeak at low speed that matches the wheels
Vibration that grows with speed
Rust dust near the driveshaft joints

tire_balance.name: Tires out of balance or damaged
tire_balance.plain: A tire is out of balance or damaged, so it wobbles at speed and you feel a shake.
tire_balance.drive: Yes. But check the tires for bulges first. A bulge can blow out.
tire_balance.todo: Ask a tire shop to balance the tires. It's quick and cheap.
tire_balance.summary: A wheel weight fell off or a tire is damaged, so the wheel wobbles at speed. You feel a shake in the steering wheel or seat, usually between 55 and 75 mph.
checks: Note the speed the shake starts. Balance problems usually show up at 55 to 70 mph and may smooth out above.
Look for a missing wheel weight, a bulge in the sidewall, or a mud-packed inner rim.
Big off-road tires on a lifted truck often need a road-force balance to ride smooth.
Check for a separated belt: run your hand over the tread for lumps or a wavy spot.
signs: Steering wheel shakes at 55 to 70 mph
Smooths out above or below that speed
Started after new tires or hitting a curb
Uneven tire wear

alignment_problem.name: Wheel alignment off
alignment_problem.plain: Your wheels aren't pointed perfectly straight, so it pulls to one side and wears tires faster.
alignment_problem.drive: Yes. It's not urgent, but it wears out tires, which are expensive.
alignment_problem.todo: Ask for a wheel alignment. Check tire pressure first; one low tire can cause a pull.
alignment_problem.summary: The wheels aren't pointed straight, so the truck pulls to one side, the steering wheel sits crooked, and the tires wear unevenly.
checks: Check tire pressures first; one low tire can cause a pull.
Look at tire wear: the inside or outside edge worn faster means camber or toe is off.
After a lift, aligning is a must. Lifts change toe and camber, and worn tie rods or idler arms on GM trucks can't hold it.
Check for a crooked steering wheel when driving straight on a flat road.
signs: Pulls to one side on a flat road
Steering wheel sits crooked
Tires wear on one edge
Started after a pothole or curb

exhaust_leak.name: Exhaust leak
exhaust_leak.plain: Exhaust gas is escaping before it should, causing a ticking or loud rumble.
exhaust_leak.drive: Yes, with windows cracked. If you smell exhaust inside, fix it fast; the fumes are dangerous.
exhaust_leak.todo: Ask a shop to find the exhaust leak. On GM trucks it's often a broken exhaust manifold bolt.
exhaust_leak.summary: Exhaust gas is escaping before the muffler. It sounds like a tick at cold start or a loud rumble, and exhaust fumes in the cab are dangerous.
checks: GM trucks: a tick at cold start that fades as it warms up is the classic broken exhaust manifold bolt. Look for black soot streaks at the manifold.
Listen under the truck for a puff or tick at each joint and the flex pipe; the leak often gets louder under load.
A leak before the O2 sensor can cause false lean codes.
If you smell exhaust in the cab, drive with windows open and get it fixed fast: carbon monoxide is deadly.
signs: Louder than normal, like a rumble
Ticking when cold
Exhaust smell inside
Black soot near a pipe joint

oil_leak_low_oil.name: Oil leak or low oil
oil_leak_low_oil.plain: The engine is losing oil or running low. Oil keeps the engine from grinding itself apart.
oil_leak_low_oil.drive: Only after you add oil to the right level. If the oil light is on, stop driving.
oil_leak_low_oil.todo: Check the oil (see the dipstick) and top it up. Then have the leak found before it gets worse.
oil_leak_low_oil.summary: Oil is leaking or running low. Low oil can ruin the engine, so check it right away if you see drips, smell burning oil, or the oil light comes on.
checks: Check the dipstick on level ground with the engine off for a few minutes; top up if it's below ADD.
Find the leak: clean the area and check common spots like the valve covers, oil pan gasket, rear main seal and oil filter.
6.0L Vortec: the oil pressure sensor behind the intake and the oil cooler lines leak often. Oil pressure about 40 to 60 psi at highway speed.
A burning oil smell after driving usually means oil dripping onto the exhaust manifold.
signs: Brown or black spots where you park
Burning oil smell after driving
Oil light flickers at stops
Blue smoke from the tailpipe

power_steering_problem.name: Power steering problem
power_steering_problem.plain: The power steering helps you turn the wheel easily. Low fluid or a weak pump makes it whine or feel heavy.
power_steering_problem.drive: Yes, but steering takes more effort, especially when parking. Get it checked soon.
power_steering_problem.todo: Check the power steering fluid level. If it's low, there's likely a leak to fix.
power_steering_problem.summary: The power steering pump, fluid or hoses are causing a whine, groan, or hard steering, often worse at low speed or when parking.
checks: Check the fluid level and color in the reservoir; dark or foamy fluid needs a flush.
A whine that rises as you turn the wheel points to the pump or low fluid.
Look for leaks at the hose fittings and the steering gear box on the frame.
Big tires on a lifted truck strain the pump and the steering box; check the box mounting bolts and frame for cracks.
signs: Whine when turning
Steering heavy at low speed
Red or clear fluid near the front
Groan when parking

ac_problem.name: A/C not cooling
ac_problem.plain: The air conditioning is low on refrigerant (the stuff that makes cold air) or a part isn't switching on.
ac_problem.drive: Yes, it's only comfort. Just stay cool in the heat.
ac_problem.todo: Ask a shop for an A/C check. Topping it off without fixing the leak only works for a while.
ac_problem.summary: The air conditioning blows warm or weak. It's usually low refrigerant from a leak, a compressor clutch that won't engage, or a blend door issue.
checks: With A/C on, see if the compressor clutch in the front of the compressor is spinning.
Check the A/C fuse and relay; the clutch needs 12V to engage.
Low side pressure about 25 to 45 psi and high side 150 to 250 psi on a warm day is normal; low readings mean a leak.
GM trucks: a clicking behind the dash is a blend door actuator; it can cause warm air on one side.
signs: Air is cool but not cold
Cold on the highway, warm at stop lights
A/C works then stops
Clicking or loud noise when the A/C turns on

electrical_ground_problem.name: Bad electrical ground or wiring
electrical_ground_problem.plain: A loose or corroded wire connection is causing weird electrical problems that come and go.
electrical_ground_problem.drive: Usually yes. But if it causes random no-starts, don't rely on it far from home.
electrical_ground_problem.todo: Ask a shop to check the ground connections. Cleaning and tightening them is often a cheap fix.
electrical_ground_problem.summary: A corroded or loose ground strap or wire causes strange electrical problems: flickering lights, gauges that jump, random no-starts, and odd warning lights.
checks: Check the engine-to-frame and battery-to-body ground straps for corrosion; clean to bare metal and tighten.
Do a voltage drop test: under 0.2V between the battery negative and the engine block while cranking.
GM trucks of this era have known instrument cluster stepper motor failures that make gauges stick or jump.
Look for chafed wires where the harness rubs on the frame, especially after a lift.
signs: Lights flicker
Gauges jump or drop
Random warning lights
Problems come and go with bumps

worn_suspension.name: Worn suspension or steering parts
worn_suspension.plain: Parts that hold the wheels and smooth out bumps are worn. You get clunks, bouncing, or loose steering.
worn_suspension.drive: Yes, carefully. Loose steering or a big wobble means slow down and get it checked soon.
worn_suspension.todo: Ask a shop for a front-end and suspension inspection. Lifted trucks wear these parts faster.
worn_suspension.summary: Worn ball joints, tie rods, idler arm, shocks or bushings cause clunks over bumps, loose steering, and a bouncy or wandering ride.
checks: Push down hard on each corner: it should bounce once and settle. More bounces mean worn shocks.
Jack up the front and rock each wheel at 9 and 3 o'clock to check tie rods, and at 12 and 6 for ball joints.
GM 2500HD idler arm and pitman arm wear out often and cause loose steering; a lift makes it worse.
Check torsion bar adjusters and sway bar links and bushings for clunks over bumps.
signs: Clunks over bumps
Bouncy or floaty ride
Nose dives when braking
Uneven tire wear

timing_chain_problem.name: Stretched timing chain
timing_chain_problem.plain: A chain inside the engine keeps the parts moving in step, like a bike chain. When it stretches, it rattles and the engine runs poorly.
timing_chain_problem.drive: Short trips only. If the chain jumps or breaks, the engine can be badly damaged.
timing_chain_problem.todo: Get it to a shop soon. Tell them it rattles for a few seconds at startup and give them any codes (like P0016 or P0008).
timing_chain_problem.summary: The timing chain or its guides and tensioner are worn, so cam timing drifts. Common on some GM 3.6L V6, Ford 3.5L/5.4L, VW/Audi 2.0T, BMW and Nissan engines.
checks: Listen at cold start: a rattle or chain slap for 2 to 10 seconds that quiets down is the classic sign.
Read codes: P0008, P0009, P0016, P0017 (cam/crank correlation) point to stretch.
Check oil level and condition; low or old oil makes chains and tensioners wear faster.
A shop can check cam timing with a scan tool (cam/crank correlation values) before opening the engine.
signs: Rattle for a few seconds at startup
Check engine light
Rough running
Rattle gets longer over time

head_gasket_failure.name: Blown head gasket
head_gasket_failure.plain: A seal inside the engine has failed, so coolant and oil can mix or leak into the cylinders. The engine overheats and can be ruined.
head_gasket_failure.drive: No. Driving with a blown head gasket can destroy the engine. Park it and get it checked.
head_gasket_failure.todo: Have a shop do a coolant pressure test and a 'block test' (checks for exhaust in the coolant). Tell them about white smoke or milky oil.
head_gasket_failure.summary: The gasket between the cylinder head and block is leaking. Often caused by overheating. Known on Subaru 2.5L, Chrysler 2.7L, some Ford, Northstar V8 and Mini engines.
checks: Look for thick white exhaust smoke that smells sweet, especially at startup.
Pull the dipstick and check under the oil cap: milky, light brown sludge means coolant in the oil.
Coolant level keeps dropping with no outside leak, or bubbles in the coolant tank while running.
A shop can do a cooling system pressure test, a combustion leak (block) test, and a compression or leak-down test.
signs: White smoke that smells sweet
Coolant keeps disappearing
Milky oil or oil cap
Overheating

catalytic_converter_problem.name: Clogged or failing catalytic converter
catalytic_converter_problem.plain: The catalytic converter cleans the exhaust. When it clogs or wears out, you may smell rotten eggs, lose power, or get a check engine light.
catalytic_converter_problem.drive: Yes for short trips if it still runs well. If it's badly clogged and has no power, get it checked; it can overheat.
catalytic_converter_problem.todo: Get the code read (P0420/P0430 is common). Fix any misfire first, because misfires ruin converters.
catalytic_converter_problem.summary: The converter is worn out or clogged, often after a long misfire or burning oil. Also a common theft target on trucks and hybrids.
checks: Read codes: P0420 or P0430 means it isn't cleaning well; misfire codes mean fix those first.
Rotten egg (sulfur) smell from the exhaust, or a rattle under the vehicle from the converter's insides breaking up.
Loss of power going uphill and a glowing red-hot converter mean it's clogged.
A shop can test exhaust back pressure or temperature before and after the converter.
signs: Rotten egg smell
Check engine light after a misfire
Feels choked or weak going uphill
Rattle under the middle of the vehicle

evap_leak.name: Gas cap or EVAP leak
evap_leak.plain: The fuel tank's vapor system has a small leak. Very often it's just a loose or worn gas cap. It turns on the check engine light but rarely affects driving.
evap_leak.drive: Yes. It's safe to drive. You may smell a little gas near the tank.
evap_leak.todo: Tighten the gas cap until it clicks. If the light stays on after a few days of driving, replace the cap ($15 to $25), then get the code read.
evap_leak.summary: The EVAP system traps fuel vapor. A loose cap, cracked hose, or stuck purge or vent valve trips codes like P0455, P0442 and P0456.
checks: Check the gas cap: tighten until it clicks, look for a cracked seal.
Read codes: P0455 (large leak), P0442/P0456 (small), P0446 (vent), P0496 (purge valve).
Smell for raw gas near the tank or filler neck after filling up.
A shop can smoke-test the EVAP system to find small hose leaks.
signs: Light came on right after getting gas
Gas cap doesn't click
Gas smell near the tank
Pump clicks off early when filling

sticking_brake_caliper.name: Sticking brake caliper
sticking_brake_caliper.plain: One brake isn't letting go all the way, so it keeps rubbing. That wheel gets very hot and can smell like burning.
sticking_brake_caliper.drive: Only a short, gentle trip to a shop. A dragging brake overheats and can make the brakes fade.
sticking_brake_caliper.todo: Ask a shop to check the brakes on the wheel that's hot or smelly. Often it's a caliper slide pin or the caliper itself.
sticking_brake_caliper.summary: A caliper piston or its slide pins are seized, so the pad keeps pressure on the rotor. Common on older vehicles and in salty areas.
checks: After a drive, carefully hold your hand near each wheel (don't touch): one much hotter than the others is the sticking one.
Look for much more brake dust on one wheel than the others.
Pulling to one side while driving or braking, and a burning smell from one corner.
A shop checks the slide pins (should move freely with grease) and that the piston retracts.
signs: One wheel is much hotter than the others
Burning smell from one corner
Pulls to one side
Much more brake dust on one wheel

bad_motor_mounts.name: Worn engine or transmission mounts
bad_motor_mounts.plain: Rubber mounts hold the engine in place. When they wear out, the engine rocks, so you feel thumps when shifting and extra shaking at stops.
bad_motor_mounts.drive: Yes, but get it checked. A badly broken mount can let the engine move too far and damage hoses or wires.
bad_motor_mounts.todo: Ask a shop to check the motor mounts. Tell them about the clunk when shifting into drive or reverse.
bad_motor_mounts.summary: Engine and transmission mounts are rubber blocks that crack and collapse with age, letting the engine move and transmit vibration.
checks: Have someone watch the engine (hood open, parking brake on, foot on the brake) while you shift between drive and reverse: a big jump means a bad mount.
Look for cracked or separated rubber on the mounts.
Vibration through the seat and steering wheel at idle in drive that smooths out in neutral.
A clunk when you step on the gas or let off quickly.
signs: Thump when shifting into drive or reverse
Extra vibration at stop lights
Clunk when you hit the gas
Engine visibly jumps when shifting

blower_motor_problem.name: Heater / A/C fan problem
blower_motor_problem.plain: The fan that pushes air out of the vents is failing. Most often the fan only works on the highest setting, or not at all.
blower_motor_problem.drive: Yes. It only affects comfort, but you need it to defrost the windshield, so fix it before winter or rain.
blower_motor_problem.todo: If it only works on high, the 'blower motor resistor' is bad: a cheap part that's often easy to swap. If nothing works, check the fuse first.
blower_motor_problem.summary: The blower motor resistor (or control module) fails, so lower speeds stop working; a worn blower motor squeals or stops.
checks: Fan only works on the highest setting: the blower resistor is the usual cause.
No fan at all: check the blower fuse, then the motor (sometimes a tap on the motor makes it run).
A squeal, rattle or ticking from behind the glove box with the fan on: leaves in the fan or a worn motor.
Weak airflow on every setting: check the cabin air filter.
signs: Fan only works on high
No air from the vents
Noise from behind the glove box
Weak airflow

clutch_problem.name: Clutch problem (stick shift)
clutch_problem.plain: On a manual (stick shift) vehicle, the clutch connects the engine to the wheels. When it wears out, the engine revs but the vehicle doesn't speed up, or gears grind.
clutch_problem.drive: Short trips if it still moves. If it slips badly or won't go into gear, it can leave you stranded.
clutch_problem.todo: Ask a shop to check the clutch. Tell them if it slips, grinds, or the pedal feels different.
clutch_problem.summary: A worn clutch disc slips; a failing hydraulic master or slave cylinder causes a soft pedal and grinding; a bad throwout bearing makes noise when the pedal is up or down.
checks: Slipping test: in a high gear at low speed, press the gas firmly. If RPM jumps but speed doesn't, the clutch is slipping.
Check the clutch fluid (often shares the brake fluid reservoir) for low level or leaks.
Pedal feels soft, sticks to the floor, or engages very high: hydraulic problem.
A burning smell (like burnt toast) after hills or traffic means it's slipping.
signs: Engine revs but you don't speed up (stick shift)
Grinding when shifting gears
Pedal feels soft or sticks
Burning smell after hills

low_tire_pressure.name: Low tire pressure or slow leak
low_tire_pressure.plain: One or more tires are low on air, often from a nail or a slow leak. The tire light comes on and the vehicle may pull slightly.
low_tire_pressure.drive: Yes, slowly, to the nearest air pump. Driving on a very low tire can ruin it and is unsafe.
low_tire_pressure.todo: Check all tires (the right number is on a sticker inside the driver's door) and add air. If one keeps losing air, a tire shop can plug or patch it, often cheaply.
low_tire_pressure.summary: Tires lose about 1 psi a month and more in cold weather; nails, bad valve stems, and rusty rims cause slow leaks.
checks: Check pressure with a gauge when tires are cold; match the door sticker, not the number on the tire.
Look for nails or screws; spray soapy water on the tread and valve stem and watch for bubbles.
Tire light comes on in cold mornings and goes off later: tires are just a little low; add air.
A tire light that flashes for a minute then stays on means a tire pressure sensor problem, not low air.
signs: Tire light on, especially on cold mornings
A tire looks flatter than the others
Pulls slightly to one side
Steering feels heavier

abs_sensor_problem.name: ABS / wheel speed sensor problem
abs_sensor_problem.plain: A sensor at one wheel tells the brakes how fast that wheel spins. When it fails, the ABS and traction lights come on.
abs_sensor_problem.drive: Yes. Your normal brakes still work, but the anti-lock brakes are off, so brake gently on slick roads.
abs_sensor_problem.todo: Get the ABS code read (many parts stores can't read ABS codes; a shop can). Often it's one wheel speed sensor or its wire.
abs_sensor_problem.summary: A wheel speed sensor, its wiring, or a rusty tone ring fails. Often tied to a wheel bearing on vehicles where the sensor is built into the hub.
checks: ABS and traction control lights on together is the classic sign.
A shop reads the ABS code to see which wheel; check that wheel's sensor wire for damage.
Speedometer acting erratic can come from the same sensors on some vehicles.
If the brake light is also on, check the brake fluid level too.
signs: ABS light on
Traction control light on too
Speedometer acting strange
Brakes feel normal otherwise

key_ignition_problem.name: Key, key fob or ignition switch problem
key_ignition_problem.plain: The vehicle doesn't recognize the key, or the key won't turn. Very often it's just a dead key fob battery or a locked steering wheel.
key_ignition_problem.drive: If it starts, yes. A failing ignition switch can stall the engine, so get it checked if it ever shuts off while driving.
key_ignition_problem.todo: Try these first: wiggle the steering wheel while turning the key, try your spare key, and replace the key fob battery (a few dollars).
key_ignition_problem.summary: Push-button cars can't detect a fob with a dead battery; worn keys or ignition cylinders won't turn; a bad ignition switch can cut power.
checks: Key won't turn: turn the steering wheel left and right while turning the key (the steering lock is on).
Push-button start with 'key not detected': hold the fob right against the start button while pressing it, then replace the fob battery.
Try the spare key. If the spare works, the first key is the problem.
Dash lights flicker or the engine cuts off when you bump the key: the ignition switch is worn.
signs: Key won't turn
'Key not detected' message
Remote buttons work only up close
Dash flickers when you bump the key

heater_core_problem.name: Leaking heater core
heater_core_problem.plain: A small radiator behind the dashboard heats the cab. When it leaks, the windows fog up, it smells sweet inside, and the floor can get wet.
heater_core_problem.drive: Short trips, yes. But watch the temperature gauge, because it's losing coolant, and the fog on the windows can block your view.
heater_core_problem.todo: Ask a shop to pressure test the cooling system. Tell them about the sweet smell inside and the foggy windows.
heater_core_problem.summary: The heater core leaks coolant into the cab, often from old coolant. Replacing it can mean removing the dashboard.
checks: A sweet, syrupy smell inside the cab with the heat on.
A greasy film on the inside of the windshield that's hard to wipe off.
Wet or damp carpet on the passenger side floor.
Coolant level dropping with no puddle under the vehicle.
signs: Sweet smell inside
Windows fog up with a greasy film
Wet carpet on the passenger side
Losing coolant with no puddle

cvt_problem.name: CVT transmission problem
cvt_problem.plain: A CVT is an automatic with no fixed gears (common on Nissan, Subaru, Honda, Toyota, Mitsubishi). When it wears, it judders, whines, or revs up without speeding up.
cvt_problem.drive: Gently, for now. Avoid hard acceleration and towing. If it goes into limp mode or slips badly, have it towed.
cvt_problem.todo: Ask a dealer if there's a software update or an extended CVT warranty for your VIN, then have the CVT fluid checked.
cvt_problem.summary: The CVT belt, pulleys or valve body are wearing or overheating: judder from a stop, a rising whine, RPM flare, or limp mode. Many makers extended CVT warranties.
checks: Read transmission codes. Nissan P17F0/P17F1 (judder), P0776, P0841 and P0868 (low fluid pressure) are common.
Check for overheating: CVT fluid temperature over about 230°F (110°C) on a scan tool puts it in limp mode.
CVT fluid is specific (Nissan NS-2/NS-3, Subaru High Torque, Honda HCF-2). The wrong fluid causes judder.
Many makers recommend a fluid change around 25,000 to 60,000 miles even if the manual says 'lifetime'.
signs: Judder or shudder when pulling away from a stop
A whine that rises as you speed up
Engine revs climb but you don't go faster
Sudden loss of power (limp mode) on long hills or hot days

torque_converter_shudder.name: Torque converter shudder
torque_converter_shudder.plain: The torque converter connects the engine to an automatic transmission. When its clutch slips and grabs, it feels like driving over rumble strips at 25 to 50 mph.
torque_converter_shudder.drive: Yes, for now. It gets worse over time and can wear the transmission, so get it looked at soon.
torque_converter_shudder.todo: Ask a shop or dealer about a transmission fluid exchange with the updated fluid (GM 8-speeds especially). If that doesn't stop it, the torque converter is replaced.
torque_converter_shudder.summary: The torque converter clutch is slipping and grabbing, usually from worn or wrong fluid. Common on GM 6L80/8L90/8L45, Ford 6F35 and older 4L60-E automatics.
checks: It happens on light gas around 25 to 50 mph, and stops when you press harder or let off. That's the torque converter clutch.
Codes P0741 (torque converter clutch stuck off) or P0796 can show up.
GM 8L90/8L45 (2015 to 2019): GM service bulletins call for a triple flush with Mobil 1 LV ATF HP fluid.
Check that the engine isn't misfiring; a misfire at cruise can feel the same. Tire balance shakes don't stop when you change throttle.
signs: Feels like rumble strips at 25 to 50 mph
Shudder on light gas that stops when you press harder
Happens on the highway when climbing a gentle hill
Engine RPM wavers a little at steady speed

water_pump_failure.name: Water pump failure
water_pump_failure.plain: The water pump pushes coolant through the engine. When its seal leaks or its bearing wears, coolant drips out at the front of the engine and it can overheat.
water_pump_failure.drive: Only if the temperature gauge stays normal and you keep coolant topped up. If it gets hot or the pump is loud, stop.
water_pump_failure.todo: Look for drips or crusty coolant below the pump at the front of the engine. Get it replaced before it overheats; if a timing belt drives it, do both together.
water_pump_failure.summary: The water pump's seal is leaking or its bearing is worn. Coolant drips at the front of the engine, the pump may whine or grind, and it can overheat.
checks: Look for a weep hole drip or dried coolant crust right under the pump pulley.
Engine off, grab the pump pulley and rock it: any wobble or grinding means a worn bearing.
Some engines (Ford 3.5/3.7, Mazda 3.7, Chrysler 2.7, GM 3.6) have the pump inside, behind the timing chain: coolant loss with no drip and milky oil.
Pressure-test the cooling system (around 15 to 18 psi for most cars) to find the leak.
signs: Coolant drips at the front of the engine
A sweet smell after driving
Low coolant light that keeps coming back
Whine or grinding from the belt area

oil_burning.name: Engine burning oil
oil_burning.plain: Some engines burn oil inside instead of leaking it out. The oil level drops between changes but there are no drips, and you may see blue smoke.
oil_burning.drive: Yes, as long as you keep the oil full. Running it low on oil is what kills the engine.
oil_burning.todo: Check the oil every time you get gas and top it up. Ask a dealer about an oil consumption test and warranty extensions; many engines had them.
oil_burning.summary: Oil is getting past worn or sticking piston rings, valve seals, or the PCV system and burning. Common on Toyota 2.4L, Subaru FB, GM 2.4L and 5.3L AFM, Honda V6 VCM, Audi 2.0T and BMW N63.
checks: No drips under the vehicle and no oil on the engine, but the level drops: it's burning, not leaking.
Pull the spark plugs: oily, black-crusted plugs show which cylinders burn oil.
A dealer oil consumption test measures how much it uses over about 1,000 miles; over a quart in 1,000 to 2,000 miles usually qualifies for warranty help.
Check the PCV valve first; a stuck one can pull oil into the intake and is cheap to replace.
signs: Need to add oil between changes
Blue-gray smoke at startup or when you step on it
Oil light flickers on turns when it's low
Oily, fouled spark plugs

throttle_body_problem.name: Dirty or failing throttle body
throttle_body_problem.plain: The throttle body is the electronic valve that lets air into the engine when you press the gas. Dirt or a failing motor makes it stall, idle wrong, or drop into reduced power.
throttle_body_problem.drive: Usually yes around town. If it goes into reduced power mode, drive gently to a shop or home.
throttle_body_problem.todo: Clean the throttle body with throttle body cleaner (engine off). If the wrench light or reduced power comes back, it needs replacing; check for warranty coverage.
throttle_body_problem.summary: Carbon on the throttle plate or a failing electronic throttle motor causes stalling, a high or low idle, slow response and reduced power (wrench light). Common on GM, Ford, Dodge and Nissan.
checks: Codes P2101, P2111, P2112, P2119, P2135 or P0121/P0122 point at the throttle body or pedal sensor.
Look inside the throttle body: a black ring around the plate causes stalling and a low idle.
After cleaning or replacing it, many need an idle relearn (key on 10 seconds, then idle for a few minutes, or a scan tool).
Ford, GM and Nissan had warranty extensions on electronic throttle bodies for some years.
signs: Wrench light or 'reduced engine power'
Stalls when coming to a stop
Idle too high or surging
Slow or no response when you press the gas

collapsed_lifter.name: Lifter or valve tick
collapsed_lifter.plain: Lifters ride on the camshaft and open the valves. When one collapses or sticks, it ticks like a sewing machine and that cylinder misfires. Very common on V8s that shut off cylinders to save gas (GM AFM/DFM, Hemi MDS).
collapsed_lifter.drive: Short trips only. A failed lifter can chew up the camshaft and turn a lifter job into an engine job.
collapsed_lifter.todo: Check the oil level first. Get it to a shop soon and tell them it ticks all the time and may misfire. Ask about recalls and warranty on GM 5.3/6.2 and Hemi engines.
collapsed_lifter.summary: A stuck or collapsed hydraulic lifter (or bad rocker/valve clearance) makes a steady tick that follows engine speed, often with a misfire on one cylinder. Common on GM AFM/DFM V8s, Chrysler Hemi and early 3.6L Pentastar.
checks: The tick stays after warm-up and speeds up with RPM. An exhaust manifold tick fades as it warms.
Read misfire codes: a single-cylinder misfire (like P0302 or P0307) plus a tick points to a lifter.
GM AFM/DFM: P3400 codes and misfires on cylinders 1, 4, 6, 7 (AFM cylinders) are a strong sign.
Use the right oil viscosity and change it on time; dirty or low oil starves the lifters.
signs: A tick that speeds up with the engine
Ticking that doesn't go away when warm
Misfire or shaking on one cylinder
Check engine light that keeps coming back

engine_knock.name: Engine knock (rod bearing)
engine_knock.plain: A deep knock from inside the engine usually means a worn rod bearing. The parts are hitting each other, and the engine can fail suddenly.
engine_knock.drive: No. Driving with a rod knock can break the engine. Have it towed.
engine_knock.todo: Turn it off and check the oil level. Have it towed to a shop. On Hyundai/Kia, GM 6.2L and other recalled engines, check your VIN; many get a free engine.
engine_knock.summary: A deep, rhythmic knock that gets faster with RPM and louder under load usually means a spun or worn rod bearing, often from low oil. Hyundai/Kia Theta II and Nu, GM 6.2L L87 and some Toyota/Lexus V6s had engine recalls.
checks: A rod knock is deep and gets louder when you rev it or load it; a lifter tick is light and steady.
Check oil pressure with a gauge; low hot-idle pressure (under about 10 psi) points to worn bearings.
Look for metal flakes in the oil or on the drain plug magnet.
Hyundai/Kia: a knock sensor detection system update was part of the recall; check for a lifetime engine warranty on your VIN.
signs: Deep knock that gets faster with the engine
Knocking louder when you accelerate
Oil light on, especially at idle
Metal flakes in the oil

turbo_problem.name: Turbocharger problem
turbo_problem.plain: A turbo uses exhaust to push extra air into the engine. When it leaks or wears, you lose power, hear a whistle or siren sound, or see smoke.
turbo_problem.drive: Gently. If you see heavy smoke or hear grinding from the turbo, stop driving; a failing turbo can send pieces into the engine.
turbo_problem.todo: Have a shop check for boost leaks (cracked hoses or intercooler) and oil leaks at the turbo. Change oil on time; old oil kills turbos.
turbo_problem.summary: Boost leaks, a sticking wastegate or worn turbo bearings cause low power, a loud whistle or siren, smoke, and code P0299 (underboost). Common on Ford EcoBoost, VW/Audi TSI, BMW N54/N55, Subaru turbos and Mazda 2.3T.
checks: Code P0299 = underboost (leak or wastegate); P0234 = overboost.
Check the intercooler hoses and clamps for oil film, cracks or loose clamps; a smoke test finds boost leaks.
Pull the intake hose at the turbo and check the shaft: in-and-out play or a chewed-up wheel means a failed turbo.
Let a hot turbo idle 30 to 60 seconds before shutting off after hard driving or towing.
signs: Loss of power when you step on it
A loud whistle or siren sound
Blue or white smoke from the exhaust
Check engine light (P0299)

diesel_emissions_problem.name: Diesel emissions (DPF / DEF / EGR) problem
diesel_emissions_problem.plain: Modern diesels clean their exhaust with a soot filter (DPF), a fluid called DEF, and an EGR system. When a sensor or part fails, the truck limits its power or speed.
diesel_emissions_problem.drive: Usually yes, but power may be cut or a countdown can limit you to 5 mph. Get it fixed before the countdown runs out.
diesel_emissions_problem.todo: Check the DEF level and quality first. Then have a diesel shop read the codes; NOx sensors, DEF heaters and clogged EGR coolers are common and well known.
diesel_emissions_problem.summary: DPF soot loading, DEF heater or NOx sensor failures, or a clogged/leaking EGR cooler set emissions codes and limp mode. Common on Duramax, Power Stroke, Cummins and EcoDiesel trucks since 2007.
checks: Codes: P2002/P2463 (DPF), P20EE (SCR efficiency), P20B9 (DEF heater), P2201 (NOx sensor), P0401/P0402 (EGR).
Watch the DPF soot load on a scan tool. Short trips stop it from regenerating; 20+ minutes on the highway helps it clean itself.
DEF goes bad when old or hot; a refractometer should read about 32.5% urea.
Losing coolant with white sweet smoke on a 6.0 or 6.4 Power Stroke (or EcoDiesel) points to a leaking EGR cooler.
signs: DEF or exhaust filter warning light
Reduced power or limp mode
A countdown message to a speed limit
Regenerating (cleaning) much more often

hybrid_ev_problem.name: Hybrid or EV system problem
hybrid_ev_problem.plain: Hybrids and electric vehicles have a big high-voltage battery, an inverter and a charger. When one has trouble, you get a 'check hybrid system' warning, less range or power, or it won't charge.
hybrid_ev_problem.drive: If it still drives normally, go straight to a dealer. If it won't go into Ready or loses power, have it towed. Never touch orange high-voltage cables.
hybrid_ev_problem.todo: Have a dealer or hybrid/EV specialist check it. Check your warranty: hybrid and EV batteries are usually covered for 8 years / 100,000 miles or more. Check for recalls too.
hybrid_ev_problem.summary: A weak high-voltage battery, failing inverter or coolant pump, or charger fault (like Hyundai/Kia ICCU) causes hybrid warnings, poor mileage or range, power loss, or charging failures.
checks: Toyota hybrids: P0A80 (replace hybrid battery) and P0A7F mean worn battery cells; check the battery cooling fan filter under the rear seat.
P0AA6 (high-voltage isolation fault) is a safety warning; don't keep driving it.
Hyundai/Kia/Genesis EVs: a 12V battery warning or loss of power can be the ICCU, which was recalled.
Check the 12V battery too; a weak 12V battery makes hybrids and EVs refuse to start.
signs: 'Check hybrid system' or EV warning
Worse gas mileage or less range
Won't go into Ready, or loses power
Won't charge, or charges very slowly

four_wheel_drive_problem.name: 4WD / AWD system problem
four_wheel_drive_problem.plain: 4WD and AWD systems send power to all wheels through a transfer case or PTU and front hubs. When a motor, actuator or gear fails, 4WD won't engage, you get a warning, or it grinds.
four_wheel_drive_problem.drive: Yes in 2WD, if it doesn't grind or bind. Don't use 4WD on dry pavement, and stop if it binds or clunks in turns.
four_wheel_drive_problem.todo: Have a shop scan the 4WD codes and check the transfer case or PTU fluid. Shift motors, actuators and vacuum lines are common, moderate fixes.
four_wheel_drive_problem.summary: A failed transfer case shift motor/encoder, front axle actuator, vacuum hub (Ford IWE), worn PTU or transfer case pump causes 4WD warnings, no engagement, grinding or binding.
checks: GM trucks: 'Service 4WD' with code C0327 (encoder) often means the transfer case encoder motor; check the connector for corrosion.
Ford F-150 IWE: grinding from the front wheels in 2WD usually means a cracked vacuum line or check valve, not the hubs.
Ford/Volvo AWD PTU: check for gear oil leaks and a burnt smell; the fluid is often never changed.
GM NP261/263 transfer cases: 'pump rub' wears a hole in the rear case; look for fluid leaks at the back of the transfer case.
signs: 4WD light flashing or 'Service 4WD'
4WD won't engage or won't come out
Grinding from the front wheels
Binding or hopping in tight turns

differential_problem.name: Differential (rear end) problem
differential_problem.plain: The differential is the gear box in the middle of the axle that turns the wheels. When its fluid is low or gears wear, it whines or howls at speed, especially on and off the gas.
differential_problem.drive: Yes, for now, if it's just a whine. If it clunks, grinds or leaks a lot, get it checked soon; a failed differential can lock up.
differential_problem.todo: Have the differential fluid level checked and changed (with friction modifier for limited slip). Fix any leaking axle or pinion seals.
differential_problem.summary: Low or worn gear oil, worn pinion bearings or gears, or leaking seals in the front or rear differential. A whine or howl that changes on and off the gas, groaning on turns, or oily axle ends.
checks: Whine that changes when you go from gas to coasting = differential gears or pinion bearing. A wheel bearing hum changes when you swerve.
Check the fill plug: fluid should be right at the bottom of the hole. Metal paste on the drain plug means wear.
Limited-slip rear ends (common on trucks) groan or chatter in tight turns without friction modifier.
Look for wet gear oil around the pinion seal (front of the axle) and the axle ends behind the wheels.
signs: Whine or howl from the rear at highway speed
Noise changes on and off the gas
Groan or chatter in tight turns
Gear oil leaking at the axle

death_wobble.name: Death wobble
death_wobble.plain: On trucks and Jeeps with a solid front axle, a worn track bar, ball joints or tie rods can let the front end shake violently after a bump. It's scary but it stops when you slow way down.
death_wobble.drive: Not until it's fixed. If it starts: grip the wheel, don't slam the brakes, and slow down gently until it stops.
death_wobble.todo: Have a shop check the track bar, ball joints, tie rods, steering box and tire balance. A new steering damper alone only hides it.
death_wobble.summary: Violent front-end oscillation after a bump at 40 to 60 mph on solid-axle trucks and Jeeps (Ram 2500/3500, Ford Super Duty, Jeep Wrangler/Gladiator). Usually a loose track bar or worn steering parts.
checks: With the engine running and someone rocking the steering wheel, watch the track bar ends for any movement.
Check ball joints, tie rod ends and the steering box mount for play; lifted trucks wear them faster.
After a lift, check caster (a shop can measure it) plus tire balance and pressure.
Jeep Wrangler JL and Gladiator had a recall for the track bar bracket weld on the frame; check your VIN.
signs: Violent steering wheel shake after hitting a bump
Only stops when you slow way down
Happens around 40 to 60 mph
Loose steering between episodes

air_suspension_problem.name: Air or electronic suspension problem
air_suspension_problem.plain: Some vehicles ride on air bags instead of metal springs. When a bag leaks or the compressor wears out, the vehicle sags, the compressor runs a lot, or a suspension warning comes on.
air_suspension_problem.drive: Short, gentle trips if it isn't sagging to the bump stops. Driving it sagged wears the compressor and makes it handle badly.
air_suspension_problem.todo: Have the leaking air spring found (spray soapy water on them) and replaced, plus the compressor relay. Coil spring conversion kits are a cheaper permanent option on some.
air_suspension_problem.summary: Leaking air springs, a worn compressor or a stuck relay cause sagging, a noisy or constantly running compressor, and suspension warnings. Common on Land Rover, Mercedes Airmatic, Lincoln/Ford, Jeep Quadra-Lift, Audi allroad, Lexus AHC and Ram.
checks: Sagging overnight at one corner = a leaking air spring or line on that corner.
Spray soapy water on the air springs and fittings with the system aired up; bubbles show the leak.
A compressor that runs for minutes or never stops can burn out; replace the relay with the compressor.
Magnetic/adaptive shocks: oily shocks and a 'service suspension' message mean a leaking shock.
signs: Sags at one corner after sitting
Compressor runs a lot or is loud
Suspension warning on the dash
Bouncy or very harsh ride

blend_door_actuator.name: Blend door actuator
blend_door_actuator.plain: Small motors behind the dash move doors that mix hot and cold air and pick the vents. When one breaks, it clicks or taps and the air gets stuck hot, cold, or on one vent.
blend_door_actuator.drive: Yes. It's annoying, not dangerous. Make sure the defroster still works in winter.
blend_door_actuator.todo: Have a shop find which actuator is clicking (the sound gives it away) and replace it. The part is inexpensive; labor depends on where it sits.
blend_door_actuator.summary: A stripped or failing HVAC door actuator behind the dash: clicking or tapping, air stuck hot or cold, wrong vents, or different temperatures on each side. Very common on GM trucks and SUVs and Ford F-150s.
checks: Clicking that starts when you turn the key or change the temperature, then stops, is a stripped actuator gear.
GM: an HVAC actuator recalibration (pull the HVAC fuse for a minute, then reinstall with everything off) can fix a confused actuator.
Stuck hot or cold on one side only means that side's temperature door actuator.
If the A/C is cold at the vents only with the temp on full cold, the A/C works; the blend door is the issue.
signs: Clicking or tapping behind the dash
Air stuck hot or stuck cold
Different temperatures on each side
Air comes out the wrong vents

instrument_cluster_problem.name: Instrument cluster / gauge problem
instrument_cluster_problem.plain: The gauges on your dash are run by small motors and sensors. When they wear, needles stick, jump around or drop to zero, even though the engine is fine.
instrument_cluster_problem.drive: Yes, but you can't trust the gauges. Watch your speed with a phone GPS app and check fuel by miles driven.
instrument_cluster_problem.todo: A cluster repair shop can replace the gauge motors for much less than a new cluster. A wrong fuel gauge only is often the fuel level sender in the tank.
instrument_cluster_problem.summary: Failed gauge stepper motors or a bad fuel level sender: speedometer, tach, fuel or temp needles stick, jump or read zero. Very common on 2003 to 2006 GM trucks and SUVs.
checks: GM 2003 to 2006: run the cluster self-test (hold the odometer button while turning the key on); a needle that doesn't sweep has a bad motor.
Only the fuel gauge wrong = test the fuel level sender resistance at the tank connector.
Several gauges dead at once with warning lights can be a bad ground or a cluster power wire.
Check the speedometer against GPS; bigger tires make it read low (common on lifted trucks).
signs: Speedometer stuck or jumping
Gas gauge reads wrong
Needles drop to zero while driving
Gauges come back after a bump

infotainment_problem.name: Touchscreen / infotainment problem
infotainment_problem.plain: The touchscreen runs the radio, maps, Bluetooth and often the backup camera. Software glitches make it freeze, reboot, go black or touch things by itself.
infotainment_problem.drive: Yes, but if the backup camera or defrost controls are on the screen, be careful when they drop out.
infotainment_problem.todo: Restart it (hold the power or volume button 10+ seconds), remove and re-pair your phone, then ask a dealer for software updates. Some screens are replaced under recall or warranty.
infotainment_problem.summary: Infotainment software or hardware faults: frozen or black screen, random reboots, ghost touches, Bluetooth/CarPlay dropping, a dead backup camera. Common across most makes since about 2010.
checks: Do a soft reset (hold power 10 to 20 seconds), then a factory reset of the radio if needed.
Ghost touches and delamination (Cadillac CUE) mean the touch layer failed; the screen is replaced.
Check the backup camera recall list; many makes recalled cameras that go blank.
A weak 12V battery causes lots of screen glitches; test the battery.
signs: Screen freezes or goes black
Radio reboots by itself
Bluetooth or CarPlay keeps dropping
Screen presses things on its own

window_regulator_problem.name: Power window regulator
window_regulator_problem.plain: The window regulator is the track and cable inside the door that lifts the glass. When it breaks, the window drops, goes up crooked, or the motor grinds.
window_regulator_problem.drive: Yes. If the window won't close, tape plastic over it or tape the glass up so it doesn't fall or let rain in.
window_regulator_problem.todo: Replace the regulator (often sold with the motor). It's an easy DIY on most vehicles: remove the door panel, unbolt it, swap it.
window_regulator_problem.summary: A broken cable, clip or motor in the window regulator: the window falls into the door, goes up crooked, moves slowly, or you hear grinding or clicking with no movement.
checks: Hear the motor run but the glass doesn't move = broken regulator cable or clips.
Nothing at all from that window = check the switch and the motor; try the master switch on the driver door.
Slow window: clean and lubricate the window channels with silicone spray.
Some makers (VW, BMW, Ford, Chrysler) have very common regulator failures; good aftermarket kits are cheap.
signs: Window fell into the door
Grinding or clicking in the door
Window goes up crooked
Window moves very slowly

door_lock_problem.name: Door lock or latch problem
door_lock_problem.plain: Each door has a small lock motor (actuator) and latch. When one fails, that door won't lock or unlock with the button, it buzzes, or it won't open. Sliding doors use cables that break.
door_lock_problem.drive: Yes, as long as every door closes and latches. A door that won't latch shut is unsafe; don't drive with it.
door_lock_problem.todo: Have the door lock actuator or latch replaced; check for door latch recalls. Sliding van doors often need a new cable or motor.
door_lock_problem.summary: A failed door lock actuator, latch, handle or power sliding door cable: doors that don't lock/unlock with the key fob, buzz, won't open, or a sliding door that sticks.
checks: One door doesn't lock with the fob but the others do = that door's lock actuator.
Buzzing or grinding in the door when you lock it = stripped actuator gears.
None lock = check the fob battery and the lock fuse first.
Power sliding doors (Honda Odyssey, Toyota Sienna, Chrysler vans) have common cable and latch recalls.
signs: One door won't lock with the button
Buzzing in the door when locking
Door won't open from inside or outside
Sliding door sticks or won't close

water_leak_inside.name: Water leak inside (sunroof drains / seals)
water_leak_inside.plain: Rain or car wash water is getting inside, usually through clogged sunroof drains or bad door and window seals. It soaks the carpet and can ruin electronics.
water_leak_inside.drive: Yes, but dry it out soon. Wet carpet grows mold, and water can short out modules under the seats or dash.
water_leak_inside.todo: Clear the sunroof drains (in each corner of the sunroof) with compressed air or a trimmer line. Check door seals and the windshield seal. Dry the carpet fully.
water_leak_inside.summary: Clogged sunroof drains or failing door, window, roof or windshield seals let water in: wet carpet, drips from the headliner, a musty smell and foggy windows, especially after rain.
checks: Pour a little water in the sunroof tray corners; it should drain out behind the front wheels or rear wheels in seconds.
Wet carpet only after rain (not after using the heater) points to a leak; sweet-smelling wet carpet is a heater core.
Run a hose over one area at a time with someone inside to find the leak.
Check under the carpet and seats for wet modules and wiring; many electrical glitches start with water.
signs: Wet carpet after rain or a car wash
Water dripping from the headliner
Musty smell inside
Water stains on the headliner

rust_damage.name: Rust damage
rust_damage.plain: Road salt and moisture eat metal. Rust on body panels is cosmetic, but rust on the frame, brake lines or suspension mounts can be dangerous.
rust_damage.drive: Yes if it's just body panels. If the frame is flaking through or has holes, have it inspected before driving it hard or towing.
rust_damage.todo: Have a shop check the frame, brake lines and suspension mounts. Treat surface rust early; wash the underside often in winter. Check for frame recalls (Toyota trucks).
rust_damage.summary: Corrosion of body panels (rockers, cab corners, wheel arches) or structural parts (frame, subframe, control arm mounts). Common on older GM and Ford trucks, Toyota Tacoma/Tundra/Sequoia frames and Mazda wheel arches.
checks: Tap the frame with a hammer: a solid ring is fine, a dull thud or flaking means it's thin.
Look at the rocker panels and cab corners from underneath; bubbles on the outside mean holes inside.
Check brake and fuel lines along the frame rails; rusted lines can burst.
Toyota Tacoma (2005 to 2010), Tundra and Sequoia had frame rust recalls and buybacks; check the VIN.
signs: Bubbling paint on the rockers or wheel arches
Holes in the cab corners
Flaking or soft frame
Orange stains under the doors

adas_problem.name: Driver-assist (auto braking) problem
adas_problem.plain: Driver-assist systems use a camera behind the windshield and a radar in the grille to brake for you. Dirt, a bad sensor or a software bug can make them brake hard for nothing.
adas_problem.drive: Yes, carefully. Many vehicles let you turn automatic emergency braking off in the settings until it's fixed.
adas_problem.todo: Clean the windshield in front of the camera and the radar sensor in the front bumper or grille. Ask a dealer for software updates and check for recalls.
adas_problem.summary: False automatic emergency braking (phantom braking) or collision warnings from a dirty, misaligned or faulty camera or radar, or software. Several makes have had investigations or recalls for it.
checks: Check for a 'front sensor blocked' message; mud, snow or a bug-covered grille blocks the radar.
After a windshield replacement or front-end repair, the camera and radar must be recalibrated.
Note when it happens (bridges, shadows, overpasses) to tell the dealer; it helps them find the software fix.
Look up the VIN for recalls on automatic emergency braking.
signs: Brakes slam on with nothing in front
Collision warning beeps for no reason
'Front sensor blocked' message
Cruise control or lane assist shuts off
